What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and soft matter systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, distinct from neighbor-based alignment.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter that can be harnessed for designing new materials and understanding biological motion.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory formation in biopolymer networks driven far from equilibrium, which is relevant to soft matter physics and biological materials.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression due to oxide coverage.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic potential landscape in graphene devices is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance, but indirect transport measurements lack spatial detail.
method: The authors employ in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution to image the valence band edge across a graphene device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: They observe up to 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene regions covered by AlOx and TiOx, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to uncover potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.

abstract: Author(s): Iris Bree, Federico Gasparotto, Antonela Matijašić, Pouria Mazloumi, Dmytro Melnichenko, Sebastian Pögel, Toni Teschke, Xing Wang, Stefan Weinzierl, Konglong Wu, and Xiaofeng Xu (
tldr: This paper presents improvements in Feynman integral reduction and epsilon-factorized differential equations for high-energy physics calculations.
motivation: Feynman integral reduction is crucial for multi-loop scattering amplitudes in particle physics, but current methods are computationally intensive.
method: The authors propose three improvements: trivializing epsilon dependence in integration-by-parts identities, optimizing prefactor choices, and streamlining the reduction process.
result: The new approach simplifies the reduction and yields epsilon-factorized differential equations more efficiently.
conclusion: These improvements enhance the practicality of Feynman integral calculations for precision phenomenology.

authors: I. Doran, L. Jeckel, M. Beyer, Ch. Jungen, And F. Merkt
abstract:

We present a general theoretical treatment and calculations of the fine and hyperfine structures in the spectra of high-[MATH] molecular Rydberg states in static uniform electric fields. The treatment combines (i) multichannel quantum-defect theory and long-range polarization models to determine the fi…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062812] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical treatment and calculations of fine and hyperfine structures in molecular Rydberg states under static electric fields.
motivation: Understanding Stark effects in molecular Rydberg states is important for spectroscopy and molecular physics, but it does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors combine multichannel quantum-defect theory with long-range polarization models to compute Stark manifolds including fine and hyperfine structures.
result: They provide detailed calculations for H2 and D2 molecules, showing how electric fields affect the energy levels and spectral features.
conclusion: The work advances molecular Rydberg spectroscopy but has no direct application to the user's research interests.

title: Hadronic Vacuum Polarization Effect In Muonic Atoms
authors: Zoia A. Mandrykina, Moritz Thierfeld, And Natalia S. Oreshkina

The hadronic vacuum polarization (HVP) corrections to energy levels in muonic atoms are studied systematically across the periodic table. [Phys. Rev. A 113, 062806] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper calculates hadronic vacuum polarization corrections to energy levels in muonic atoms across the periodic table.
motivation: Precision spectroscopy of muonic atoms requires accurate QED corrections, including hadronic vacuum polarization, to test fundamental physics.
method: Two nuclear charge distribution models are used: a homogeneously charged sphere (partly analytical) and a more realistic Fermi distribution (numerical integration).
result: Systematic HVP corrections are computed for muonic atoms from Z=1 to Z=100, showing dependence on nuclear size and model.
conclusion: The results provide improved theoretical predictions for muonic atom energy levels, aiding future experiments.

motivation: To understand and model X-ray scattering from vicinal surfaces during heteroepitaxial growth, which is important for characterizing thin film structures.
method: Theoretical formalism incorporating film-induced interference fringes, elastic lattice distortion, terrace ordering, surface reconstruction, and real-time growth.
result: Provides a comprehensive scattering theory that can be used to analyze experimental CTR data from vicinal surfaces.
conclusion: The theory enables detailed structural characterization of strained heteroepitaxial films on vicinal substrates.

title: Topological Enhancement Of Protein Kinetic Stability
authors: João N. C. Especial And Patrícia F. N. Faísca
abstract:
Author(s): João N. C. Especial and Patrícia F. N. Faísca

Knotted proteins embed a physical (i.e., open) knot within their native structures. For decades, significant effort has been devoted to elucidating the functional role of knots in proteins, yet no consensus has been reached. Here, using extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple struc…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, L062402] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how topological knots in proteins enhance their kinetic stability using Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: To understand the functional role of knots in proteins, which has remained unclear despite decades of research.
method: Extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple structure-based model for knotted proteins.
result: Topological knots significantly increase the kinetic stability of proteins by slowing down unfolding.
conclusion: Knots may serve a biological function by enhancing protein robustness against mechanical or thermal stress.

title: Force And Geometric Signatures Of The Creep-to-failure Transition In A Granular Pile
authors: Qing Hao, Luca Montoya, Elena Lee, Luke K. Davis, And Cacey Stevens Bester
abstract:
Author(s): Qing Hao, Luca Montoya, Elena Lee, Luke K. Davis, and Cacey Stevens Bester

This paper presents experiments on a quasi-two-dimensional pile of photoelastic disks and investigates the microscopic structural and dynamical changes underlying granular creep and the signatures of the creep-to-failure transition. The experiments report rearrangement, force, and geometric events before macroscopic grain motion at the surface is observed, indicating that subtle rearrangements in the force chain network precede macroscopic failure.

#ClearMotivation #ElegantVisuals


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065417] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies granular creep and failure in a photoelastic disk pile, focusing on force chain rearrangements before macroscopic failure.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic precursors to failure in granular materials is important for predicting landslides and structural collapses.
method: Experiments on a quasi-2D pile of photoelastic disks track force chains and geometric rearrangements via imaging and stress analysis.
result: Subtle rearrangements in the force chain network precede macroscopic surface motion, providing early signatures of failure.
conclusion: The creep-to-failure transition in granular piles can be detected through internal force and geometric changes before visible failure.

title: Global Buckley-Leverett Theory For Multicomponent Flow In Fractured Media: Isothermal Equation-of-state Coupling And Dynamic Capillarity
abstract:
Author(s): Christian Tantardini and Fernando Alonso-Marroquín

We present an isothermal global Buckley-Leverett framework for multicomponent, multiphase flow in porous and fractured media that retains the interpretability of classical Buckley-Leverett while incorporating essential physics: equation-of-state-based phase behavior, multicomponent Maxwell-Stefan di…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065106] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper extends the Buckley-Leverett theory to multicomponent, multiphase flow in fractured media with equation-of-state coupling and dynamic capillarity.
motivation: Classical Buckley-Leverett theory lacks the ability to handle multicomponent phase behavior and dynamic capillary effects, which are important for realistic reservoir simulation.
method: The authors develop a global framework that integrates equation-of-state-based phase behavior, multicomponent Maxwell-Stefan diffusion, and dynamic capillarity into the Buckley-Leverett formulation.
result: The framework retains interpretability while capturing essential physics of multicomponent flow in fractured porous media.
conclusion: The proposed model provides a more accurate description of multiphase flow in fractured reservoirs, with potential applications in enhanced oil recovery and CO2 sequestration.

result: Characterization of secondary-ion emission dynamics and correlations with cluster impact parameters.

#AdvancingField #TechnicalAdvancement


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064127] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a statistical closure scheme for stellar dynamics around a supermassive black hole using the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism.
motivation: To understand the dynamics of stars orbiting a supermassive black hole and test statistical closure schemes in the nonlinear regime.
method: An iterative scheme based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism is developed and compared with numerical simulations.
result: The iterative scheme compares well with numerical simulations.
conclusion: The proposed closure scheme is effective for calculating dynamical correlation functions in this astrophysical context.

The Jeans instability in an unmagnetized, collisionless self-gravitating plasma characterized by a kappa or Lorentzian velocity distribution is investigated in the framework of kinetic and fluid approaches. We have examined the role of suprathermality on the instability threshold wave number and gro…

result: Suprathermality modifies the instability threshold wave number and growth rate.

result: Facilitating compression yields effects on displacement patterns.

conclusion: High-purity X-ray polarimetry is a powerful tool for studying electronic anisotropies in metal-containing materials, with potential applications in chemistry and materials science.

method: A PLASEN system combining a radio-frequency quadrupole cooler buncher with collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy was developed and tested with radioactive beams.
result: The setup was successfully commissioned, demonstrating its capability for high-resolution spectroscopy of exotic nuclei.

authors: Christian S. Kern, Xiaosheng Yang, Giovanni Zamborlini, Simone Mearini, Matteo Jugovac, Vitaliy Feyer, Umberto de Giovannini, Angel Rubio, Serguei Soubatch, Michael G. Ramsey, F. Stefan Tautz, And Peter Puschnig

Circular dichroism in the angular distribution (CDAD) is the effect that the angular intensity distribution of photoemitted electrons depends on the handedness of the incident circularly polarized light. The origin of CDAD can be manifold, including intrinsic properties of the system under study, su…

tldr: This paper studies circular dichroism in photoelectron angular distribution from achiral molecules, a phenomenon in photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Understanding the origin of circular dichroism in photoelectron angular distributions from achiral molecules, which can arise from experimental geometry or final-state effects.
method: Combined experimental measurements using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and theoretical simulations based on one-step photoemission model.
result: Observed circular dichroism in the photoelectron angular distribution from achiral molecules, attributed to the experimental geometry and final-state scattering effects.
conclusion: The circular dichroism effect in achiral molecules is a geometric effect, not related to molecular chirality, and must be accounted for in chiral molecule studies.

Using a linear hydrodynamic model, we theoretically investigate the interaction between penetrating electron beams and sub-5-nm metallic spherical nanoparticles. authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism can improve reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: A multi-step process involving surface defects, electrical stress, heating, and particle emission triggers breakdown.
conclusion: Improved understanding can lead to more reliable and efficient high-power technologies and advanced accelerators.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the universe, and their properties constrain the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is important for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from gravitational-wave signals of binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical predictions of the nuclear equation of state.
result: The measurements provide constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, which are compared to extrapolations of nuclear equation of state calculations.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of dense matter, but the paper does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights capabilities and limitations of each technique and cases where they are combined.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques provide direct access to atomic-scale disorder, and combining them yields a more comprehensive understanding.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions in stars is crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions on Earth.
result: Provides a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical phenomena dominate stellar nuclear reactions, and new experimental methods are needed to study them.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, focusing on the generation and use of maximally localized Wannier functions.
result: It describes the ecosystem's capabilities for computing band structures, topological invariants, and other properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

title: Electron Spin Drift In Long-distance Plasma Wakefield Acceleration
authors: Ming Zeng And Dazhang Li Yilan Guo
abstract: Plasma based wakefield acceleration of polarized electron beams has recently attracted considerable research interest. Previous works have found the forced spin oscillation of electrons due to two-dimensional betatron oscillation in particle trajectory and discovered longitudinal depolarization mechanism in plasma wakefield. In this work, we present a three-dimensional analytical model for the electron spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration. Our analysis reveals several phenomena including a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of the drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization. This work can offer guidance on future plasma-based accelerators for polarized electron beams.
tldr: This paper presents a three-dimensional analytical model for electron spin dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration, focusing on spin drift and polarization evolution.
motivation: Polarized electron beams are important for high-energy physics, and plasma-based accelerators offer compact acceleration but may depolarize the beam; understanding spin dynamics is crucial.
method: The authors develop a 3D analytical model for electron spin evolution during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration, incorporating betatron oscillations and wakefield effects.
result: They find a transverse rotational spin drift causing depolarization, a reversal of drift frequency, and subsequent polarization recovery.
conclusion: The work provides guidance for designing plasma-based accelerators that preserve electron beam polarization.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for analyzing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand nontrivial physics beyond planarity in gauge/gravity duality by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden defect extension of 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel double-particle operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in conformal field theories.

conclusion: These results contribute to the understanding of cosmic ray composition and propagation, but are unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

abstract:

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 241802] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses PandaX-4T double beta decay data to search for scalar-mediated interactions between neutrinos and dark matter.
motivation: To probe exotic scalar-mediated interactions among neutrinos and dark matter particles using direct detection data.
method: Performs a spectral search in double beta decay data from the PandaX-4T experiment.
result: Sets constraints on scalar-neutrino and scalar-dark-matter couplings.
conclusion: The PandaX-4T data provide new limits on these interactions, but no evidence is found.

abstract:

tldr: This paper computes leading effective field theory corrections to the Kerr metric for all spins using numerical methods.
motivation: To parametrize and compute corrections to general relativity from higher-derivative interactions in a low-energy effective field theory, agnostic to UV completion.
method: Numerical methods are used to solve the modified field equations and compute corrections to the Kerr metric.
result: The leading-order corrections to the Kerr metric are obtained for all spins.
conclusion: The results provide a general parametrization of deviations from general relativity in black hole spacetimes.

title: First Experimental Limit On The Permanent Electric Dipole Moment Of The Deuteron
abstract:
Author(s): A. Andres et al. (JEDI Collaboration)

tldr: This paper reports the first experimental limit on the permanent electric dipole moment (EDM) of the deuteron, probing CP-violating physics beyond the Standard Model.
motivation: Permanent EDMs are sensitive probes of new CP-violating physics that could explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe. Measuring the deuteron EDM provides unique constraints on CP violation in the strong and weak sectors.
method: The JEDI Collaboration used a storage ring technique to measure the spin precession of deuterons in a magnetic field, searching for a signal of an EDM.
result: They set a new upper limit on the deuteron EDM, improving previous bounds and constraining theoretical models of CP violation.
conclusion: The result provides the first experimental limit on the deuteron EDM, demonstrating the feasibility of storage-ring EDM searches and setting important constraints on beyond-Standard-Model physics.

title: Observation Of The Radiative Decay ${D}_{s0}^{*}(2317{)}^{+}→{D}_{s}^{*+}γ$
abstract:

tldr: Observation of the radiative decay of an exotic meson, D_s0*(2317)+ → D_s*+ γ, providing insight into its internal structure.

result: The radiative decay is observed, and the branching fraction is measured.

title: Laser-Plasma Based Seeded Free Electron Laser In The High-Gain Regime
authors: Marie Labat, Susanne Schöbel, Amin Ghaith, Franziska Marie Herrmann, Maxwell Laberge, Eléonore Roussel, Ulrich Schramm, Patrick Ufer, Marie-Emmanuelle Couprie, And Arie Irman
abstract:

The realization of compact laser-plasma accelerator (LPA) driven free electron lasers (FELs) has been attempted for nearly two decades, yet, difficult to overcome electron beam quality and stability issues prevented FEL lasing until recently. LPA based FEL is now demonstrated in both the self-amplif…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 245001] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a laser-plasma accelerator driven free electron laser operating in the high-gain regime, a milestone in compact FEL technology.
motivation: Laser-plasma accelerators offer compact electron sources but have faced beam quality issues preventing FEL lasing; this work aims to overcome those challenges.
method: The authors use a laser-plasma accelerator to generate electron beams and inject them into an undulator to achieve seeded FEL amplification in the high-gain regime.
result: They report successful FEL lasing with high gain, demonstrating the viability of LPA-driven FELs.
conclusion: This achievement marks a significant step toward compact, table-top free electron lasers for applications in ultrafast science and imaging.

title: Ablating Pellets For Areal Density Symmetry Control In Indirectly Driven Inertial Confinement Fusion Target Designs
authors: O. A. Hurricane, D. J. Strozzi, S. A. Maclaren, And C. Weber
abstract:

While ignition has been achieved on the National Ignition Facility (NIF), implosion symmetry was not perfect, an…

tldr: This paper presents a method using ablating pellets to control areal density symmetry in indirectly driven inertial confinement fusion implosions.
motivation: Asymmetry in compressed fusion fuel configuration limits performance in inertial confinement fusion; achieving ignition requires better symmetry control.
method: The authors propose and simulate the use of ablating pellets placed strategically to modify the radiation drive and improve areal density symmetry.
result: Simulations show that ablating pellets can reduce areal density variations, potentially improving implosion performance.
conclusion: Ablating pellets offer a viable technique for symmetry control in ICF target designs, which may help achieve higher yields.

title: Tangential Forces Govern The Viscous-Inertial Transition In Dense Frictional Suspensions
authors: Sudarshan Konidena, Franco Tapia, Alireza Khodabakhshi, Élisabeth Guazzelli, Pascale Aussillous, And Bernhard Vowinckel

We present particle-resolved simulations of dense frictional suspensions undergoing the viscous-inertial transition using pressure-imposed rheology. By varying the fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular pressure, we demonstrate that the transition occurs at a Stokes number of [MATH] (close to the v…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 248201] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the viscous-inertial transition in dense frictional suspensions using particle-resolved simulations, focusing on tangential forces.
motivation: Understanding the transition from viscous to inertial regimes in dense suspensions is important for industrial and natural processes, but the role of tangential forces was unclear.
method: Particle-resolved simulations with pressure-imposed rheology were performed, varying fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular pressure to isolate the effect of tangential forces.
result: The transition occurs at a Stokes number close to the viscous-inertial crossover, and tangential forces are found to govern the transition.
conclusion: Tangential forces are key to the viscous-inertial transition in dense frictional suspensions, providing a mechanistic understanding.

title: Recoil Corrections To Muonic Hydrogen Hyperfine Splitting

method: The authors compute quantum electrodynamic and recoil corrections directly, and use the hydrogen hyperfine splitting to estimate proton structure corrections.
result: They present a complete theory of the hyperfine splitting including all contributions above 1 ppm.
conclusion: The work provides a refined theoretical value for muonic hydrogen hyperfine splitting, aiding tests of bound-state QED and proton structure.

title: Structural And Vibrational Properties Of Multialkali Antimonide Photocathode Thin Films Studied By Raman Spectroscopy And Density Functional Theory Calculations

result: They identify conditions for multistability and characterize bifurcation diagrams showing transitions between different stable states.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the design principles of multistable gene circuits, which can inform synthetic biology.

title: Influence Of Visual Field Offset On Collective Behavior: An Exploration Using The Two-dimensional Vicsek Model
authors: Poorendra Ramlall, Sachit Butail, And Subhradeep Roy

method: Agent-based simulations of the two-dimensional Vicsek model with a parameterized visual field offset angle.
result: Visual field offset alters the order-disorder transition and can enhance or hinder collective alignment depending on the offset angle and noise level.
conclusion: The offset of visual field is a significant factor in collective behavior, with potential implications for designing robotic swarms and understanding animal groups.

result: The paper outlines opportunities to move from descriptive studies to mechanistic understanding and design of adaptive nanoparticle gels.
conclusion: Multiscale dynamics in colloidal gels can be better understood through integrated experimental and computational approaches enabled by next-generation X-ray sources.

conclusion: The work provides insights into the dynamics of chimera states on curved surfaces, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Flow Of Yield Stress Fluid In A Percolating Network

method: The authors use a pore network model with uniformly distributed throat radii and block a fraction of the largest radii, then simulate the flow of a Bingham fluid through the percolating cluster.

result: The electron beam induces phase transitions in the dust cluster, altering its crystalline structure.
conclusion: High-energy pulsed electron beams can be used to control phase transitions in complex plasma dust clusters, offering a new tool for studying condensed matter in plasma environments.

result: Optimized shock timing leads to enhanced performance in terms of yield and compression.
conclusion: Shock timing optimization is a viable route to improve shock-augmented ignition performance.

method: The authors experimentally and theoretically investigate the effect of a single microparticle placed on a surface on the dynamics of an impacting droplet, analyzing contact time reduction.
result: The presence of a microparticle significantly reduces droplet contact time by altering the droplet's spreading and retraction dynamics.
conclusion: Using a predeposited microparticle offers a simple, low-cost method to regulate droplet contact time without modifying the entire surface.

method: Numerical simulations of compressible turbulent channel flow with spanwise wall oscillations, analyzing amplitude variation effects on drag and heat transfer.

tldr: This paper studies plasma flow generation and particle acceleration from expanding magnetic bubbles using simulations and experiments.
motivation: To understand impulsive plasma dynamics driven by rising electric currents, which are relevant to astrophysical and laboratory plasmas.
method: Fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations and laser-driven capacitor-coil experiments.
result: A rising current expels plasma and generates expanding magnetic bubbles that accelerate particles.
conclusion: The findings provide quantitative understanding of plasma response to rising currents, with implications for astrophysical phenomena.

title: Leidenfrost Hydrogels: Elastic Surface-wave Instability And Sustained Bouncing
authors: Nathan C. J. Coombs, Peter Lewin-Jones, Mykyta V. Chubynsky, And James E. Sprittles
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan C. J. Coombs, Peter Lewin-Jones, Mykyta V. Chubynsky, and James E. Sprittles

This work investigates the oscillatory dynamics and subsequent sustained bouncing behavior of Leidenfrost hydrogels, a phenomenon that has received little theoretical attention to date. Building on previous approaches toward drop impacts and Leidenfrost drops, a computational model is developed to capture the oscillatory dynamics and analyze the mechanism of energy injection that leads to sustained bouncing.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022052] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the oscillatory dynamics and sustained bouncing of Leidenfrost hydrogels using computational modeling.
motivation: The phenomenon of Leidenfrost hydrogels has received little theoretical attention, and understanding the energy injection mechanism for sustained bouncing is of interest.
method: A computational model is developed to capture the oscillatory dynamics and analyze the mechanism of energy injection.
result: The model reproduces the sustained bouncing behavior and reveals the role of elastic surface-wave instability.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical insight into a novel bouncing regime for soft materials on hot surfaces.

title: Tracking Phase Synchronization Between Flagella In The Time-frequency Domain Resolves Photophobic Response
authors: Lucas Federspiel, Jorge Arrieta, Marco Polin, Françoise Argoul, And Antoine Allard
abstract:
Author(s): Lucas Federspiel, Jorge Arrieta, Marco Polin, Françoise Argoul, and Antoine Allard

The unicellular microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (CR) is well known for its biflagellated swimming in response to light stimuli. This work aims to study the resynchronization of CR flagella after a high light intensity stimulus, known as photoshock. The synchronization is estimated thanks to a qu…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023294] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies flagellar synchronization in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii using time-frequency analysis to understand photophobic response.
motivation: Understanding how microalgae coordinate flagella after light stimuli is important for biology but not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors use time-frequency domain analysis to track phase synchronization between two flagella during photoshock.
result: They resolve the resynchronization dynamics of flagella after high-intensity light stimulus.
conclusion: The work provides insights into biological synchronization but has no connection to the user's research interests.

title: When Surface Dynamics Fakes Symmetry: Oxygen On Rh(100) Revisited
authors: Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, And M. Alexander Schneider
abstract:
Author(s): Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, and M. Alexander Schneider

Heating a long-range ordered adsorbate phase beyond its stability temperature does not necessarily result in a disordered phase; it can also break up into heavily fluctuating ordered domains. Temporal and/or spatial averaging over these fluctuations may give the impression of both a wrong periodicit…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023296] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies oxygen adsorption on Rh(100) surface, revealing that fluctuating ordered domains can mimic a wrong surface symmetry under thermal averaging.
motivation: To understand the behavior of adsorbate phases beyond their stability temperature and the misinterpretation of surface symmetry due to temporal/spatial fluctuations.
method: Combined experimental techniques (STM, LEED) and theoretical modeling (Monte Carlo simulations) to analyze the surface structure and dynamics.
result: Heating the ordered oxygen phase leads to heavily fluctuating domains that, upon averaging, appear to have a different periodicity than the true local structure.
conclusion: Surface dynamics can fake symmetry, highlighting the need for careful interpretation of averaged surface measurements.

title: Controlled Interference Of Laser-induced Shock Waves In Microdroplet Jetting
authors: R. A. Meijer, G. Lajoinie, B. Liu, S. Witte, And O. O. Versolato
abstract:
Author(s): R. A. Meijer, G. Lajoinie, B. Liu, S. Witte, and O. O. Versolato

We report the formation of high-velocity microjets driven by the interference of two laser-induced shock waves in a tin microdroplet. A first 0.4-ns laser pulse launches a shock wave into the droplet (diameter [MATH], 50, and [MATH]). Due to the droplet's s…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023287] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies laser-induced shock waves in tin microdroplets to produce high-velocity microjets, with applications in extreme ultraviolet lithography.
motivation: To understand and control the formation of microjets from laser-driven droplets, which is relevant for industrial applications like EUV light sources.
method: Two laser pulses are used to create interfering shock waves in a tin microdroplet, and the resulting jet dynamics are observed with high-speed imaging.
result: The interference of shock waves can be tuned to control the jet velocity and direction, achieving high-speed microjets.
conclusion: Controlled interference of laser-induced shock waves enables precise microdroplet jetting, with potential for optimizing EUV lithography sources.

title: Sea-surface Retention Effect Shapes Ocean Microplastic Fibers
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Mazzino and Giuseppe Suaria

Microfibers contaminate the global ocean, but their impact depends on length-dependent residence at the air-sea interface. In the submillimeter range, the sea surface exhibits a surface-enrichment signature: The long-to-short fiber ratio is higher at the interface than a few meters below (about 5 m)…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023283] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the retention of microplastic fibers at the sea surface, finding that longer fibers are enriched at the air-sea interface compared to subsurface waters.
motivation: Microplastic fibers are a major pollutant in the ocean, but their vertical distribution and residence time at the sea surface are poorly understood, which affects their environmental impact.
method: The authors combine field measurements of fiber length distributions at the sea surface and at 5 m depth with a theoretical model of fiber rise velocity and turbulent mixing.
result: They observe a higher ratio of long to short fibers at the surface than at depth, indicating a surface-enrichment effect that depends on fiber length.
conclusion: The sea surface selectively retains longer microplastic fibers, which has implications for their transport, degradation, and ecological effects.

title: Super-resonance: Breaking The Bandwidth Limit Of Resonant Modes And Its Application To Flow Control
authors: Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, And Mahmoud I. Hussein
abstract:
Author(s): Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, and Mahmoud I. Hussein

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021045] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces super-resonance, a phenomenon that breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes, and applies it to flow control.
motivation: Conventional resonance has a limited bandwidth, which restricts applications like flow stabilization. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors theoretically and numerically demonstrate super-resonance in a mechanical/acoustic system, showing how a broadband out-of-phase response can be achieved beyond the typical resonance bandwidth.
result: Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization.
conclusion: Super-resonance provides a new paradigm for resonant systems with potential applications in flow control and other areas requiring broadband response.

title: Erratum: Opposite Effects Of The Rotational And Translational Energy On The Rates Of Ion-Molecule Reactions Near 0 K: The ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{NH}}_{3}$ And ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{ND}}_{3}$ Reactions [Phys. Rev. X 14, 011034 (2024)]

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 029901] Published Wed May 20, 2026.

motivation: The original paper studied rotational and translational energy effects on ion-molecule reactions near 0 K; the erratum corrects errors in that work.
method: The erratum likely corrects data or analysis from the original experimental or theoretical study.
result: The erratum provides corrected results for the D2+ + NH3 and D2+ + ND3 reactions.
conclusion: The corrected findings refine the understanding of low-temperature ion-molecule reaction dynamics.

title: Stretching Theory Of Hookean Metashells
abstract:
Author(s): Luca Giomi

A continuum theory that describes how mechanical metamaterials deform on surfaces takes the form of the Schrödinger equation and provides a different path for materials design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021035] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: A continuum theory for mechanical metamaterials on surfaces is formulated, resembling the Schrödinger equation.
motivation: To develop a theoretical framework for designing mechanical metamaterials that deform on curved surfaces.
method: Derives a continuum theory analogous to the Schrödinger equation for Hookean metashells.
result: The theory provides a new path for materials design by linking deformation to quantum-like equations.
conclusion: The approach offers a different perspective for engineering mechanical metamaterials.

title: Using Folded Proteins As Mechanically Well-Defined Units To Understand Fatigue Fracture In Hydrogels: Bridging Single Molecule And Bulk Studies
authors: Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, And Hai Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, and Hai Lei

A force-response model helps understand fatigue behavior and provides a design strategy for fatigue resistant hydrogels and soft materials.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021031] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fatigue fracture in hydrogels using folded proteins as mechanically well-defined units, bridging single-molecule and bulk experiments.
motivation: Understanding fatigue fracture in soft materials is crucial for designing durable hydrogels, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: The authors use folded proteins as model units to probe mechanical fatigue at the single-molecule level and relate it to bulk hydrogel behavior.
result: They develop a force-response model that explains fatigue behavior and provides design principles for fatigue-resistant hydrogels.
conclusion: The work offers a strategy to engineer hydrogels with improved fatigue resistance by controlling protein unfolding and refolding dynamics.

title: Hydroplasticity Of Nanocrystal Films Induced By Mesopore Change
authors: Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, And Kai Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, and Kai Zhang

A vapor training process allows for improved plasticity and better shaping of wood-derived films.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021026] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the hydroplasticity of nanocrystal films induced by mesopore change, focusing on wood-derived films and vapor training processes.
motivation: To improve the plasticity and shaping of wood-derived films for practical applications.
method: A vapor training process is used to induce mesopore changes in nanocrystal films.
result: The process leads to improved plasticity and better shaping of the films.
conclusion: The vapor training method effectively enhances the mechanical properties of wood-derived nanocrystal films.

title: Tracking Ultrafast Ion Diffusion Dynamics In ${\mathrm{AgCrSe}}_{2}$ Superionic Conductor
authors: Jianmin Yang, Lin Xie, Mingyuan Hu, Yingpeng Qi, Jun Li, Baohai Jia, Jianghe Feng, Zijing Chen, Michel Bosman, Dao Xiang, And Jiaqing He
abstract:
Author(s): Jianmin Yang, Lin Xie, Mingyuan Hu, Yingpeng Qi, Jun Li, Baohai Jia, Jianghe Feng, Zijing Chen, Michel Bosman, Dao Xiang, and Jiaqing He

Direct spatial and temporal characterization of ion diffusion in superionic conductors provides a better link to macroscopic properties and high-performance material design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021024] Published Fri May 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies ultrafast ion diffusion dynamics in a superionic conductor using experimental techniques.
motivation: Understanding ion diffusion in superionic conductors is important for designing high-performance materials.
method: The authors use direct spatial and temporal characterization methods to track ion motion.
result: They provide detailed dynamics of ion diffusion in AgCrSe2.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of ion transport in superionic conductors.

title: Cell Bulging And Extrusion In A Three-Dimensional Bubbly Vertex Model For Curved Epithelial Sheets
authors: Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, And Ulrich S. Schwarz

Author(s): Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, and Ulrich S. Schwarz

Cells at topological defects in curved epithelial sheets experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021023] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies cell bulging and extrusion in curved epithelial sheets using a three-dimensional bubbly vertex model.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces at topological defects in curved epithelial sheets lead to cell extrusion is important for tissue biology and disease.
method: The authors develop a three-dimensional bubbly vertex model to simulate curved epithelial sheets and analyze cell shape changes and extrusion events.
result: They find that cells at topological defects experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion, and the model captures the dynamics of cell bulging and removal.
conclusion: The bubbly vertex model provides insights into the role of geometry and mechanics in epithelial tissue homeostasis and extrusion.

title: Seeing New Depths: Three-Dimensional Flow Of A Free-Swimming Alga
authors: Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, And Xiang Cheng
abstract:
Author(s): Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, Van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, and Xiang Cheng

Experimental three-dimensional measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga reveal that microscopic organisms generate unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena, expanding our understanding of microhydrodynamics with profound biological implications for microbial motility and physiology.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021019] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents experimental 3D measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga, revealing unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena.
motivation: Understanding microhydrodynamics of swimming microorganisms is important for biology and fluid dynamics, but the paper has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors used experimental three-dimensional flow measurements around a free-swimming alga.
result: They discovered unexpected flow structures at low Reynolds numbers that expand current understanding of microhydrodynamics.
conclusion: The findings have implications for microbial motility and physiology, but are unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Boosting The Thermoelectric Performance Of $α$-MgAgSb Through Phase-Transition-Induced Self-Doping
authors: Kaiwei Guo, Tianyu Wang, Zhen Fan, Lunhua He, Fuhong Chen, Yi Wang, Qi Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Hangtian Zhu, Jun Li, Te-Huan Liu, And Huaizhou Zhao
abstract:
